title: GHA Simulation #3 — Collaboration & Learning
description: A fresh general-workplace set with more emphasis on communication, collaboration, feedback, inclusion, and adaptability.

metadata.notes: Original practice content inspired by publicly reported GHA formats. Not official Google questions.

sections.name: Work Style — Most Like Me / Least Like Me
sections.instructions: For each set of three statements, choose the statement that is MOST like you and the statement that is LEAST like you.

sections.name: Work Style — Agreement Scale
sections.instructions: Choose the response that best reflects how you generally behave at work.

questions.text: Once I have invested heavily in a plan, I prefer to keep it even when priorities change.
I share context that could help teammates make better decisions.
I break complex problems into smaller questions that can be tested.
I think about edge cases when they could materially change the outcome.
When I strongly believe I am right, I have little reason to revisit my view after hearing colleagues.
If a shortcut is unlikely to be noticed, I am comfortable using it to save time.
When time is short, I tend to rely on people whose opinions I already know.
I am less likely to challenge a dismissive comment if the person who made it is influential.
I consider how my decisions affect the final outcome, not only my assigned deliverable.
I summarize decisions so that people know what will happen next.
If I expect a delay, I communicate it before the deadline is missed.
Once I become competent at a task, I rarely seek feedback on how I perform it.
I make reversible decisions promptly when additional analysis is unlikely to change the choice.
I am willing to discard work when new evidence shows that a different approach is better.
People I work with generally know what they can expect from me and when.
I delay sharing bad news until I have a complete solution.
A rule can be ignored if everyone involved informally agrees it is unnecessary.
I change my approach when credible feedback reveals a weakness.
I prefer roles where priorities remain stable for long periods.
I make important assumptions explicit when they could affect a decision.
I would correct the record if I received credit for someone else's work.
If everyone has the same formal opportunity to speak, I do not need to think further about inclusion.
I look for evidence that could challenge my first hypothesis.
I am willing to change my approach when a teammate presents stronger evidence.
Unclear ownership usually makes me pause until someone assigns responsibilities explicitly.
Once I complete my assigned part, I rarely check whether the broader outcome succeeded.
I actively look for lessons after something does not go as expected.
I sometimes avoid making a decision because I do not want to be responsible if it turns out poorly.
I would rather wait for certainty than make a reversible decision with incomplete information.
When I identify an important risk, I make sure it is visible to the right people.

sections.name: Workplace Judgment
sections.instructions: For each scenario, choose the action you would be MOST likely to take and the action you would be LEAST likely to take.

questions.scenario: A teammate strongly prefers a familiar tool, while a newer option may fit the problem better.

actions.text: Compare the options against the actual requirements and run a small test if the tradeoff is unclear.
Use the familiar tool to avoid debate.
Use the newer tool because newer technologies are usually better.
Ask management to choose the tool.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You receive conflicting requests from two stakeholders with similar authority.

actions.text: Clarify the underlying goals and priorities, make the conflict visible, and align on a decision.
Work on whichever request arrived first.
Try to satisfy both without telling them about the conflict.
Wait until one stakeholder follows up again.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A teammate consistently delivers good work but rarely shares progress until the end.

actions.text: Discuss the impact of late visibility and agree on a lightweight update rhythm.
Leave it alone because the final work is good.
Start monitoring the teammate closely without discussing it.
Escalate immediately to their manager.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: Your first solution works but creates noticeably higher operating cost than expected.

actions.text: Quantify the impact and decide whether optimization is warranted based on the real tradeoffs.
Ignore the cost because the functional requirement is met.
Rewrite everything immediately for maximum efficiency.
Hide the cost until someone asks.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A peer gives you feedback you think is based on incomplete information.

actions.text: Ask questions to understand their perspective, add missing context, and consider whether any part of the feedback is still useful.
Dismiss the feedback because the peer does not know the full situation.
Accept all of it without discussion.
Tell other teammates why the feedback was unfair.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You notice that only a few people dominate recurring team discussions.

actions.text: Adjust facilitation so relevant input can come from more people, including asynchronously when useful.
Assume the quieter people will speak if they have something important to add.
Require everyone to speak for the same amount of time.
Ask the most senior person to decide faster.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A project has multiple plausible paths and no obvious best option.

actions.text: Define decision criteria, identify what is reversible, and choose a path with a plan to learn quickly.
Continue researching until one option becomes clearly superior.
Pick the option you know best.
Ask several stakeholders to vote without defining criteria.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You are asked to summarize an incident before the investigation is complete.

actions.text: Separate confirmed facts from hypotheses and clearly label what remains unknown.
Provide the most likely explanation so leaders have a simple answer.
Refuse to share anything until the investigation is complete.
Share every theory discussed by the team.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A teammate accidentally deletes work and is embarrassed to tell the team.

actions.text: Help recover or recreate the work, encourage early disclosure, and focus on preventing recurrence rather than blame.
Keep it secret if the work can be recreated before anyone notices.
Tell the team immediately without giving the teammate a chance to explain.
Let the teammate solve it alone so they learn from the mistake.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: An internal process requires a form that seems redundant for your specific case.

actions.text: Follow the process or use the approved exception path while proposing an improvement if the redundancy is real.
Skip the form because the requirement does not add value here.
Ask a colleague to submit it under their name.
Complain about the process but complete it incorrectly.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A customer reports a problem that you cannot reproduce.

actions.text: Gather more context, look for differences in environment or usage, and avoid assuming the report is wrong.
Close the issue because you cannot reproduce it.
Tell the customer to try again later.
Implement a speculative fix without understanding the cause.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A manager changes priorities after you have already completed significant work.

actions.text: Clarify the reason for the change, preserve anything reusable, and re-plan around the new priority.
Argue to keep the old priority because of the work already invested.
Switch immediately without checking what commitments are affected.
Continue the old work quietly until it is finished.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A teammate proposes using user data for a purpose that was not part of the original approved plan.

actions.text: Pause and verify whether the new use is permitted before proceeding.
Proceed if the data stays inside the company.
Use only a small sample so the risk is low.
Proceed now and ask for approval later.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You need input from an expert who is difficult to reach.

actions.text: Prepare a focused question, use available documentation and colleagues first, then contact the expert with clear context.
Wait until the expert becomes available.
Make assumptions without documenting them.
Escalate to the expert's manager immediately.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A problem reappears after your team believed it was fixed.

actions.text: Reopen the investigation, examine why the previous fix was insufficient, and update prevention measures.
Apply the same fix again because it worked before.
Treat it as a new unrelated issue.
Wait for a larger impact before spending more time on it.
